questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — During a secondary-school biology lab, two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) are crossed. What are the offspring genotype and phenotype ratios?

options.a: 1 : 2 : 1 (genotype AA : Aa : aa) and 3 : 1 (phenotype dominant : recessive)
options.c: All dominant

questions.explanation: Monohybrid cross Aa × Aa gives offspring genotype ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, and phenotype ratio 3 dominant (A_) : 1 recessive (aa).

questions.questionText: Scenario #2 — During a secondary-school biology lab, according to the 10% rule in ecosystems, what fraction of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?

options.a: Energy increases at higher trophic levels
options.b: 100% of energy is transferred
options.c: Approximately 10% of energy is passed from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat, in undigested matter, or used in respiration
options.d: All energy passes to decomposers only

questions.explanation: Energy flow in ecosystems: about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (10% rule). The rest is lost as heat (respiration), in undigested waste, or used for life processes. This is why food chains typically have only 4–5 trophic levels.

questions.questionText: Scenario #3 — During a secondary-school biology lab, a test cross is performed between a heterozygous parent (Aa) and a homozygous recessive (aa). What fraction of the offspring will be heterozygous?

options.a: All offspring are heterozygous (Aa)
options.b: 25% heterozygous (Aa) and 75% homozygous recessive (aa)
options.c: 75% homozygous dominant (AA)
options.d: 50% heterozygous (Aa) and 50% homozygous recessive (aa)

questions.explanation: Cross Aa × aa (test cross): parental gametes (A, a) × (a) → offspring Aa, Aa, aa, aa. Probability of heterozygous Aa = 1/2 (50%); probability of homozygous aa = 1/2 (50%).

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes eutrophication in a freshwater lake?

options.a: Excess nitrates and phosphates (from fertilisers/sewage) cause algal blooms; algae die and decompose by aerobic bacteria, depleting oxygen and killing aquatic life
options.b: Eutrophication is caused by adding oxygen to lakes
options.c: Eutrophication means fish become larger
options.d: Eutrophication only happens in the ocean

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — During a secondary-school biology lab, where is the hormone adrenaline produced in the human body?

options.a: Thyroid gland (in the neck)
options.b: Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)
options.c: Adrenal glands (situated above the kidneys)
options.d: Pituitary gland (at the base of the brain)

questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is produced by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of each kidney. It increases heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose in 'fight or flight' situations.

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes Mendel's Law of Segregation?

options.a: Law of segregation: each individual has two alleles for a trait which separate during gamete formation; each gamete carries only one allele
options.b: All traits are determined by one allele only
options.c: Genes cannot be inherited from parents
options.d: All alleles always stay together in gametes

questions.explanation: Mendel's First Law (Law of Segregation): every individual possesses two alleles for each trait, and these alleles separate (segregate) during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele. The zygote restores the pair at fertilisation.

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes the process of natural selection as proposed by Darwin?

options.a: All organisms survive equally well
options.b: Variation in populations → struggle for existence → survival of the fittest → reproduction of the better-adapted organisms
options.c: Evolution happens only in bacteria
options.d: Offspring always inherit characteristics acquired during life

questions.explanation: Natural selection (Darwin): (1) populations show variation; (2) there is a struggle for existence (competition for resources); (3) the best-adapted individuals survive and reproduce; (4) their favourable traits are passed to offspring; (5) over generations, the population becomes better adapted to its environment.

options.a: Cloning produces genetically identical copies of an organism (asexual reproduction) or cell
options.b: Cloning is impossible in mammals
options.c: Cloning always involves two parents
options.d: Only plants can be cloned

questions.explanation: Cloning: producing genetically identical organisms from a single parent. Examples: asexual reproduction (binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation); somatic cell nuclear transfer (e.g., Dolly the sheep); tissue culture (plant cuttings in lab).

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly distinguishes continuous variation from discontinuous variation?

options.a: Continuous variation shows a range of phenotypes (e.g., height, weight); discontinuous variation shows distinct categories (e.g., blood group, tongue-rolling)
options.b: Continuous variation has distinct categories
options.c: Both types only depend on environment
options.d: Discontinuous variation is influenced by many genes

questions.explanation: Continuous variation: a range of phenotypes with no discrete categories (influenced by many genes + environment); examples: height, weight, skin colour, leaf length. Discontinuous variation: discrete categories (one or few genes); examples: ABO blood group, tongue-rolling ability, seed shape, presence/absence of dimples.

options.d: Recombinant DNA technology joins DNA from two different species to produce a desired gene product (e.g., human insulin produced by bacteria)

questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA technology: cutting DNA from two different organisms with restriction enzymes, joining them with DNA ligase, and inserting the recombinant DNA into a host cell (e.g., bacteria) to produce useful proteins (e.g., human insulin, growth hormone).

options.a: Haemophilia is autosomal recessive

options.d: All sex-linked traits affect females only

questions.explanation: Sex-linked traits (X-linked recessive) such as haemophilia and colour blindness: heterozygous females (X^H X^h) are carriers (phenotypically normal but carry one allele); males (X^h Y) express the trait. Cross X^H X^h × X^H Y → 1/4 X^h Y (affected male).

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, how does antibiotic resistance develop in bacterial populations?

options.a: All bacteria develop resistance after one exposure to antibiotics
options.b: Bacteria become resistant by becoming larger
options.c: Resistance is caused by drinking antibiotics
options.d: Some bacteria have natural resistance; antibiotics kill susceptible ones; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly describes codominance?

options.a: One allele completely masks the other
options.b: Codominance results in incomplete dominance (blending)
options.c: All codominant alleles produce recessive phenotypes
options.d: Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (e.g., ABO blood group AB, where both A and B antigens are present)

questions.explanation: Codominance: both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (no dominant/recessive relationship). Example: ABO blood groups — IAIA = A, IBIB = B, IAIB = AB (both A and B antigens expressed). This is different from incomplete dominance, where traits blend.

options.b: Zea mays — a two-part Latin name: genus (capital) + species (lower case), usually italicised
options.c: A single word in any language
options.d: Zea Mays — both capitalised

questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus): each species is given a two-part Latin name. The first word (capitalised) is the genus; the second word (lower case) is the specific epithet. Both are italicised or underlined, e.g., Zea mays (corn).

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — In a mangrove swamp study, which of the following describes how a nerve impulse is transmitted across a synapse?

options.a: Electric current flows directly from one neurone to another without any gap
options.b: Two neurones fuse together permanently
options.c: Messages are transmitted only by sound waves
options.d: A neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine) diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the next neurone

questions.explanation: Synapses are tiny gaps between two neurones. An electrical impulse arrives at the axon terminal, triggers release of neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine), which diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the next neurone, generating a new impulse.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — In a mangrove swamp study, which of the following correctly describes sexually transmitted infections (STIs)? — at the national park?

options.a: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as HIV/AIDS, syphilis and gonorrhoea are spread through unprotected sexual contact
options.b: STIs only affect elderly people
options.c: STIs are caused by polluted water
options.d: All STIs can be cured by drinking antibiotics once

questions.explanation: STIs are infections transmitted through sexual contact (vaginal, anal, oral). Examples: HIV/AIDS, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia. Prevention: abstinence, faithful relationships, condoms, and early screening/treatment.

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — In a mangrove swamp study, which of the following is an example of asexual reproduction?

options.a: Cross-pollination in flowers
options.b: Binary fission in Amoeba
options.c: Fertilisation in mammals
options.d: Sexual reproduction in humans

questions.explanation: Binary fission in Amoeba. Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and produces offspring that are genetically identical (clones). Examples: binary fission (Amoeba, Paramecium), budding (Hydra, yeast), spore formation (Rhizopus, fern), and vegetative propagation (ginger, potato).

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — In a mangrove swamp study, what is the function of insulin in the human body?

options.a: Insulin lowers blood glucose levels by promoting glucose uptake into body cells
options.b: Insulin raises blood glucose levels by stimulating glycogen breakdown
options.c: Insulin breaks down proteins in muscle
options.d: Insulin increases heart rate during exercise

questions.explanation: Insulin is secreted by the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake into cells (especially muscle and fat cells) and conversion to glycogen in the liver.

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — In a mangrove swamp study, which of the following correctly describes cloning in biology? — at the national park?

options.a: Cloning is impossible in mammals
options.b: Cloning always involves two parents
options.c: Cloning produces genetically identical copies of an organism (asexual reproduction) or cell
options.d: Only plants can be cloned

questions.explanation: Cloning: producing genetically identical organisms from a single parent. Examples: asexual reproduction (binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation); somatic cell nuclear transfer (e.g., Dolly the sheep); tissue culture (plant cuttings in lab).

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — In a mangrove swamp study, according to the 10% rule in ecosystems, what fraction of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?

options.a: Approximately 10% of energy is passed from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat, in undigested matter, or used in respiration
options.b: 100% of energy is transferred
options.c: All energy passes to decomposers only
options.d: Energy increases at higher trophic levels

questions.explanation: Energy flow in ecosystems: about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (10% rule). The rest is lost as heat (respiration), in undigested waste, or used for life processes. This is why food chains typically have only 4–5 trophic levels.

questions.questionText: Scenario #11 — In a mangrove swamp study, which of the following correctly compares Darwin's and Lamarck's theories of evolution?

options.a: Lamarck proposed natural selection; Darwin proposed inheritance of acquired characteristics
options.b: Darwin's theory was based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics
options.c: Both Darwin and Lamarck proposed identical theories
options.d: Darwin's theory of natural selection states that organisms with favourable variations survive and reproduce; Lamarck's theory (now rejected) stated that acquired characteristics during life could be passed to offspring

questions.explanation: Darwin's natural selection: individuals with favourable variations (arising randomly) survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest); over generations, the favourable trait accumulates in the population. Lamarck's (rejected) inheritance of acquired characteristics: features developed during life (e.g., giraffe's long neck from stretching) are passed to offspring.

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a mangrove swamp study, how does antibiotic resistance develop in bacterial populations?

options.a: Bacteria become resistant by becoming larger
options.b: All bacteria develop resistance after one exposure to antibiotics
options.c: Some bacteria have natural resistance; antibiotics kill susceptible ones; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring
options.d: Resistance is caused by drinking antibiotics

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — In a mangrove swamp study, which of the following correctly describes the process of natural selection as proposed by Darwin?

options.a: All organisms survive equally well
options.b: Evolution happens only in bacteria
options.c: Offspring always inherit characteristics acquired during life
options.d: Variation in populations → struggle for existence → survival of the fittest → reproduction of the better-adapted organisms

questions.explanation: Natural selection (Darwin): (1) populations show variation; (2) there is a struggle for existence (competition for resources); (3) the best-adapted individuals survive and reproduce; (4) their favourable traits are passed to offspring; (5) over generations, the population becomes better adapted to its environment.

options.d: In-situ conservation (e.g., national parks, wildlife reserves) protects species in their natural habitats; ex-situ conservation (e.g., zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks) protects species outside their natural habitats

questions.explanation: In-situ conservation: protecting species in their natural habitats (national parks like Taman Negara, wildlife reserves, marine parks). Ex-situ conservation: protecting species outside their natural habitats (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, captive breeding programmes). Both are important for biodiversity.

questions.questionText: Scenario #15 — In a mangrove swamp study, what are the sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms?

options.a: Variation is caused only by environment
options.b: Variation cannot be inherited
options.c: Genetic variation arises from sexual reproduction (crossing over, random assortment of chromosomes), random fertilisation and mutation
options.d: Variation is caused only by mutation

questions.explanation: Genetic variation arises from three sources: (1) crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, (2) random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. Mutation creates new alleles. Environmental factors also contribute.

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — At a national park visitor centre, what is meant by the term 'homeostasis' in human biology?

options.a: The maintenance of a stable internal environment (constant body temperature, pH, water balance and glucose level) despite external changes
options.b: The continuous increase in body size over time
options.c: The breakdown of food in the digestive tract
options.d: The release of hormones from the pituitary gland

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions to keep them stable despite external changes. Examples: thermoregulation (constant body temperature), osmoregulation (water balance), and blood glucose regulation (insulin + glucagon).

options.d: Producer (autotroph) → Primary consumer (herbivore) → Secondary consumer (carnivore) → Tertiary consumer → Decomposer

questions.explanation: Trophic levels in a food chain: Producers (green plants, photosynthetic) → Primary consumers (herbivores that eat plants) → Secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) → Tertiary consumers (top predators) → Decomposers (bacteria, fungi that break down dead matter).

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — At a national park visitor centre, which of the following correctly distinguishes continuous variation from discontinuous variation?

options.a: Continuous variation shows a range of phenotypes (e.g., height, weight); discontinuous variation shows distinct categories (e.g., blood group, tongue-rolling)
options.b: Both types only depend on environment
options.c: Continuous variation has distinct categories
options.d: Discontinuous variation is influenced by many genes

questions.explanation: Continuous variation: a range of phenotypes with no discrete categories (influenced by many genes + environment); examples: height, weight, skin colour, leaf length. Discontinuous variation: discrete categories (one or few genes); examples: ABO blood group, tongue-rolling ability, seed shape, presence/absence of dimples.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — At a national park visitor centre, which of the following correctly describes codominance?

options.a: All codominant alleles produce recessive phenotypes
options.b: Codominance results in incomplete dominance (blending)
options.c: Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (e.g., ABO blood group AB, where both A and B antigens are present)
options.d: One allele completely masks the other

questions.explanation: Codominance: both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (no dominant/recessive relationship). Example: ABO blood groups — IAIA = A, IBIB = B, IAIB = AB (both A and B antigens expressed). This is different from incomplete dominance, where traits blend.

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — At a national park visitor centre, which of the following correctly describes sex-linked inheritance?

options.a: Sex-linked traits are carried on the Y chromosome only
options.b: All sex-linked traits affect females only
options.c: A carrier female (X^H X^h) crossed with a normal male (X^H Y) gives 1/4 affected male offspring
options.d: Haemophilia is autosomal recessive

questions.explanation: Sex-linked traits (X-linked recessive) such as haemophilia and colour blindness: heterozygous females (X^H X^h) are carriers (phenotypically normal but carry one allele); males (X^h Y) express the trait. Cross X^H X^h × X^H Y → 1/4 X^h Y (affected male).

questions.explanation: Human development stages: zygote (single cell after fertilisation) → morula (solid ball) → blastocyst (hollow ball, implants in uterus) → embryo (weeks 2–8) → foetus (week 9 to birth) → baby.

options.b: Eutrophication is caused by adding oxygen to lakes
options.c: Eutrophication means fish become larger
options.d: Eutrophication only happens in the ocean

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

options.c: Progesterone and oestrogen are produced by the pancreas

questions.explanation: FSH and LH are gonadotrophic hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. FSH stimulates follicle development and oestrogen secretion; LH triggers ovulation and stimulates the corpus luteum to produce progesterone.

options.d: Recombinant DNA cannot produce useful products

questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA technology: cutting DNA from two different organisms with restriction enzymes, joining them with DNA ligase, and inserting the recombinant DNA into a host cell (e.g., bacteria) to produce useful proteins (e.g., human insulin, growth hormone).

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — In a school garden experiment, which of the following correctly describes Mendel's Law of Segregation?

options.b: All alleles always stay together in gametes
options.c: All traits are determined by one allele only
options.d: Law of segregation: each individual has two alleles for a trait which separate during gamete formation; each gamete carries only one allele

questions.explanation: Mendel's First Law (Law of Segregation): every individual possesses two alleles for each trait, and these alleles separate (segregate) during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele. The zygote restores the pair at fertilisation.

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.explanation: Genetic variation arises from three sources: (1) crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, (2) random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. Mutation creates new alleles. Environmental factors also contribute.

questions.explanation: Blood glucose regulation uses negative feedback: a rise in blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion (lowering glucose), while a fall stimulates glucagon secretion (raising glucose). This keeps blood glucose within a narrow range (~4–7 mmol/L).

questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus): each species is given a two-part Latin name. The first word (capitalised) is the genus; the second word (lower case) is the specific epithet. Both are italicised or underlined, e.g., Zea mays (corn).

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a genetics laboratory, a test cross is performed between a heterozygous parent (Aa) and a homozygous recessive (aa). What fraction of the offspring will be heterozygous?

options.b: All offspring are heterozygous (Aa)

options.d: 25% heterozygous (Aa) and 75% homozygous recessive (aa)

questions.explanation: Cross Aa × aa (test cross): parental gametes (A, a) × (a) → offspring Aa, Aa, aa, aa. Probability of heterozygous Aa = 1/2 (50%); probability of homozygous aa = 1/2 (50%).

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — In a genetics laboratory, which of the following correctly describes the process of natural selection as proposed by Darwin? — context 52?

options.a: Evolution happens only in bacteria
options.b: Offspring always inherit characteristics acquired during life

questions.explanation: Natural selection (Darwin): (1) populations show variation; (2) there is a struggle for existence (competition for resources); (3) the best-adapted individuals survive and reproduce; (4) their favourable traits are passed to offspring; (5) over generations, the population becomes better adapted to its environment.

questions.explanation: Synapses are tiny gaps between two neurones. An electrical impulse arrives at the axon terminal, triggers release of neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine), which diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the next neurone, generating a new impulse.

options.b: The continuous increase in body size over time
options.c: The breakdown of food in the digestive tract
options.d: The release of hormones from the pituitary gland

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions to keep them stable despite external changes. Examples: thermoregulation (constant body temperature), osmoregulation (water balance), and blood glucose regulation (insulin + glucagon).

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — At an urban community garden, what is the correct order of trophic levels in a typical food chain? — at the greenhouse?

options.a: Producer → Secondary consumer → Primary consumer
options.b: Only producer and consumer exist
options.c: Producer (autotroph) → Primary consumer (herbivore) → Secondary consumer (carnivore) → Tertiary consumer → Decomposer
options.d: Decomposer → Producer → Consumer

questions.explanation: Trophic levels in a food chain: Producers (green plants, photosynthetic) → Primary consumers (herbivores that eat plants) → Secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) → Tertiary consumers (top predators) → Decomposers (bacteria, fungi that break down dead matter).

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — At an urban community garden, which of the following correctly distinguishes continuous variation from discontinuous variation? — at the greenhouse?

options.a: Discontinuous variation is influenced by many genes
options.b: Continuous variation shows a range of phenotypes (e.g., height, weight); discontinuous variation shows distinct categories (e.g., blood group, tongue-rolling)
options.c: Both types only depend on environment
options.d: Continuous variation has distinct categories

questions.explanation: Continuous variation: a range of phenotypes with no discrete categories (influenced by many genes + environment); examples: height, weight, skin colour, leaf length. Discontinuous variation: discrete categories (one or few genes); examples: ABO blood group, tongue-rolling ability, seed shape, presence/absence of dimples.

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — At an urban community garden, a test cross is performed between a heterozygous parent (Aa) and a homozygous recessive (aa). What fraction of the offspring will be heterozygous?

options.a: 75% homozygous dominant (AA)
options.b: 50% heterozygous (Aa) and 50% homozygous recessive (aa)
options.c: All offspring are heterozygous (Aa)
options.d: 25% heterozygous (Aa) and 75% homozygous recessive (aa)

questions.explanation: Cross Aa × aa (test cross): parental gametes (A, a) × (a) → offspring Aa, Aa, aa, aa. Probability of heterozygous Aa = 1/2 (50%); probability of homozygous aa = 1/2 (50%).

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — At an urban community garden, what is the function of insulin in the human body?

options.b: Insulin breaks down proteins in muscle

questions.explanation: Insulin is secreted by the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake into cells (especially muscle and fat cells) and conversion to glycogen in the liver.

options.b: One allele completely masks the other

options.c: Recombinant DNA means DNA from the same individual

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — In a backyard ecosystem study, which of the following correctly compares Darwin's and Lamarck's theories of evolution? — in the home garden?

options.c: Darwin's theory was based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics

questions.explanation: Synapses are tiny gaps between two neurones. An electrical impulse arrives at the axon terminal, triggers release of neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine), which diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the next neurone, generating a new impulse.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse effect: short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth's surface and is re-emitted as long-wave infrared (heat). Enhanced greenhouse effect (excess CO₂ from burning fossil fuels, deforestation) → global warming → climate change.

options.b: When blood glucose rises, insulin is released to lower it; when blood glucose falls, glucagon is released to raise it
options.c: Hormones are produced in the adrenal glands only
options.d: Insulin raises blood glucose

questions.explanation: Blood glucose regulation uses negative feedback: a rise in blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion (lowering glucose), while a fall stimulates glucagon secretion (raising glucose). This keeps blood glucose within a narrow range (~4–7 mmol/L).

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — In a research microscope facility, which of the following correctly describes cloning in biology?

options.a: Cloning produces genetically identical copies of an organism (asexual reproduction) or cell
options.b: Only plants can be cloned
options.c: Cloning is impossible in mammals
options.d: Cloning always involves two parents

questions.explanation: Cloning: producing genetically identical organisms from a single parent. Examples: asexual reproduction (binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation); somatic cell nuclear transfer (e.g., Dolly the sheep); tissue culture (plant cuttings in lab).

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — In a research microscope facility, in the menstrual cycle, what is ovulation?

options.a: The fertilisation of an ovum by sperm
options.b: The release of a mature ovum (egg) from the ovary around day 14
options.c: The shedding of the uterine lining
options.d: The development of the corpus luteum only

questions.explanation: The release of a mature ovum (egg) from the ovary around day 14 — standard KSSM Form 5 reproductive biology.

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — In a research microscope facility, which of the following correctly describes sex-linked inheritance?

options.a: Haemophilia is autosomal recessive
options.b: All sex-linked traits affect females only
options.c: Sex-linked traits are carried on the Y chromosome only
options.d: A carrier female (X^H X^h) crossed with a normal male (X^H Y) gives 1/4 affected male offspring

questions.explanation: Sex-linked traits (X-linked recessive) such as haemophilia and colour blindness: heterozygous females (X^H X^h) are carriers (phenotypically normal but carry one allele); males (X^h Y) express the trait. Cross X^H X^h × X^H Y → 1/4 X^h Y (affected male).

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — In a research microscope facility, which of the following correctly describes the female reproductive structure of a flower?

options.a: Stigma (sticky, receives pollen) — Style (tube leading to ovary) — Ovary (contains ovules)
options.b: Sepal (sticky, receives pollen) — Receptacle (tube leading to ovary) — Anther (contains ovules)
options.c: Petal (sticky, receives pollen) — Sepal (tube leading to ovary) — Stamen (contains ovules)
options.d: Anther (sticky, receives pollen) — Filament (tube leading to ovary) — Petal (contains ovules)

questions.explanation: Female reproductive parts (pistil/carpel): stigma (sticky tip that receives pollen) — style (slender tube) — ovary (contains ovules). Male parts: anther (produces pollen) — filament.

questions.questionText: Scenario #9 — In a research microscope facility, which of the following correctly describes the greenhouse effect? — in the field?

options.a: Greenhouse effect is caused by the ozone hole only
options.b: Only CO₂ affects the climate
options.c: Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere, leading to global warming and climate change
options.d: Greenhouse gases cool the Earth

questions.explanation: Greenhouse effect: short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth's surface and is re-emitted as long-wave infrared (heat). Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour) absorb and re-emit this heat, keeping Earth warm. Enhanced greenhouse effect (excess CO₂ from burning fossil fuels, deforestation) → global warming → climate change.

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — In a research microscope facility, what are the sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms?

options.a: Variation cannot be inherited
options.b: Variation is caused only by mutation
options.c: Genetic variation arises from sexual reproduction (crossing over, random assortment of chromosomes), random fertilisation and mutation
options.d: Variation is caused only by environment

questions.explanation: Genetic variation arises from three sources: (1) crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, (2) random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. Mutation creates new alleles. Environmental factors also contribute.

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a research microscope facility, which of the following correctly compares Darwin's and Lamarck's theories of evolution?

options.a: Darwin's theory of natural selection states that organisms with favourable variations survive and reproduce; Lamarck's theory (now rejected) stated that acquired characteristics during life could be passed to offspring
options.b: Both Darwin and Lamarck proposed identical theories
options.c: Darwin's theory was based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics
options.d: Lamarck proposed natural selection; Darwin proposed inheritance of acquired characteristics

questions.explanation: Darwin's natural selection: individuals with favourable variations (arising randomly) survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest); over generations, the favourable trait accumulates in the population. Lamarck's (rejected) inheritance of acquired characteristics: features developed during life (e.g., giraffe's long neck from stretching) are passed to offspring.

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — In a research microscope facility, which of the following hormones are secreted by the anterior pituitary gland to regulate the menstrual cycle?

options.a: FSH (follicle stimulating hormone) and LH (luteinising hormone) are produced by the anterior pituitary gland
options.b: Progesterone and oestrogen are produced by the pancreas
options.c: Insulin and glucagon regulate the menstrual cycle
options.d: Adrenaline and thyroxine cause ovulation

questions.explanation: FSH and LH are gonadotrophic hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. FSH stimulates follicle development and oestrogen secretion; LH triggers ovulation and stimulates the corpus luteum to produce progesterone.

questions.questionText: Scenario #14 — In a research microscope facility, what is the correct sequence of stages in ecological succession?

options.a: Pioneer community → Climax community → Intermediate
options.b: All stages occur simultaneously
options.c: Climax community → Pioneer community → Intermediate
options.d: Pioneer community → Intermediate community → Climax community

questions.explanation: Ecological succession on bare ground (e.g., after a volcanic eruption or glacier retreat): pioneer species (lichens, mosses) colonise first → intermediate communities (grasses, herbs) → shrubs → climax community (stable, mature forest). Each stage modifies the environment, allowing the next community to develop.

questions.questionText: Scenario #15 — In a research microscope facility, what is the difference between in-situ and ex-situ conservation?

options.a: Conservation refers only to animal species
options.b: Only ex-situ conservation is used in Malaysia
options.c: In-situ conservation (e.g., national parks, wildlife reserves) protects species in their natural habitats; ex-situ conservation (e.g., zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks) protects species outside their natural habitats
options.d: Both mean the same thing

questions.explanation: In-situ conservation: protecting species in their natural habitats (national parks like Taman Negara, wildlife reserves, marine parks). Ex-situ conservation: protecting species outside their natural habitats (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, captive breeding programmes). Both are important for biodiversity.

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes sexually transmitted infections (STIs)?

options.a: STIs are caused by polluted water
options.b: All STIs can be cured by drinking antibiotics once
options.c: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as HIV/AIDS, syphilis and gonorrhoea are spread through unprotected sexual contact
options.d: STIs only affect elderly people

questions.explanation: STIs are infections transmitted through sexual contact (vaginal, anal, oral). Examples: HIV/AIDS, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia. Prevention: abstinence, faithful relationships, condoms, and early screening/treatment.

questions.questionText: Scenario #2 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes genetically modified (GM) food? — context 37?

options.a: GM (genetically modified) foods contain genes from another species, introduced using recombinant DNA technology, to give desirable traits (e.g., pest resistance, longer shelf life)
options.b: GM foods are produced by selective breeding only
options.c: GM foods contain no DNA
options.d: GM foods are always more nutritious

questions.explanation: Genetically modified (GM) foods: contain one or more genes transferred from another species, conferring desirable traits (e.g., Bt corn with bacterial Bt gene for pest resistance; golden rice with added β-carotene for vitamin A). Controversies: unknown long-term health effects, environmental risks, ethical concerns.

questions.questionText: Scenario #3 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly distinguishes continuous variation from discontinuous variation?

options.a: Continuous variation shows a range of phenotypes (e.g., height, weight); discontinuous variation shows distinct categories (e.g., blood group, tongue-rolling)
options.b: Continuous variation has distinct categories
options.c: Both types only depend on environment
options.d: Discontinuous variation is influenced by many genes

questions.explanation: Continuous variation: a range of phenotypes with no discrete categories (influenced by many genes + environment); examples: height, weight, skin colour, leaf length. Discontinuous variation: discrete categories (one or few genes); examples: ABO blood group, tongue-rolling ability, seed shape, presence/absence of dimples.

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes the divisions of the human nervous system?

options.a: Lungs and liver
options.b: Central nervous system (brain + spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system
options.c: Heart and blood vessels
options.d: Stomach and intestines

questions.explanation: The human nervous system is divided into: (1) Central Nervous System (CNS) — brain and spinal cord, which integrate and process information; (2) Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — During a secondary-school biology lab, two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) are crossed. What are the offspring genotype and phenotype ratios?

options.a: 1 : 2 : 1 (genotype AA : Aa : aa) and 3 : 1 (phenotype dominant : recessive)
options.b: All dominant

questions.explanation: Monohybrid cross Aa × Aa gives offspring genotype ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, and phenotype ratio 3 dominant (A_) : 1 recessive (aa).

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes eutrophication in a freshwater lake?

options.a: Excess nitrates and phosphates (from fertilisers/sewage) cause algal blooms; algae die and decompose by aerobic bacteria, depleting oxygen and killing aquatic life
options.b: Eutrophication is caused by adding oxygen to lakes
options.c: Eutrophication means fish become larger
options.d: Eutrophication only happens in the ocean

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — During a secondary-school biology lab, a test cross is performed between a heterozygous parent (Aa) and a homozygous recessive (aa). What fraction of the offspring will be heterozygous?

options.a: 75% homozygous dominant (AA)
options.b: 25% heterozygous (Aa) and 75% homozygous recessive (aa)
options.c: 50% heterozygous (Aa) and 50% homozygous recessive (aa)
options.d: All offspring are heterozygous (Aa)

questions.explanation: Cross Aa × aa (test cross): parental gametes (A, a) × (a) → offspring Aa, Aa, aa, aa. Probability of heterozygous Aa = 1/2 (50%); probability of homozygous aa = 1/2 (50%).

questions.questionText: Scenario #9 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly defines a gene mutation? — context 85?

options.a: Mutation only occurs in muscle cells
options.b: Mutation is a sudden change in the DNA sequence that may be inherited
options.c: Mutation is the normal process of cell division
options.d: Mutation is the gradual growth of an organism

questions.explanation: Mutation is a sudden, permanent change in the DNA sequence of a gene. Types: gene mutation (change in DNA base sequence) and chromosomal mutation (change in chromosome structure/number). Mutations can be inherited (if they occur in gametes) or cause genetic disorders.

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — During a secondary-school biology lab, asexual reproduction involves?

options.a: Only one parent; offspring are genetically identical to the parent
options.b: Cross-pollination
options.c: Two parents; offspring are genetically different from parents
options.d: Gamete formation and fertilisation

questions.explanation: Only one parent; offspring are genetically identical to the parent. Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and produces offspring that are genetically identical (clones). Examples: binary fission (Amoeba, Paramecium), budding (Hydra, yeast), spore formation (Rhizopus, fern), and vegetative propagation (ginger, potato).

options.a: Producer → Secondary consumer → Primary consumer

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly describes the 5-kingdom classification of living organisms?

options.a: Two kingdoms: prokaryotes and eukaryotes only
options.b: Three kingdoms: animal, plant, fungi
options.c: Seven kingdoms (all sub-categories)
options.d: The 5-kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia

questions.explanation: The 5-kingdom classification (Whittaker): Monera (prokaryotes: bacteria, cyanobacteria); Protista (protozoans, algae); Fungi (mushrooms, yeast); Plantae (plants); Animalia (animals).

questions.questionText: Scenario #2 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, how does antibiotic resistance develop in bacterial populations?

options.a: All bacteria develop resistance after one exposure to antibiotics
options.b: Some bacteria have natural resistance; antibiotics kill susceptible ones; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring
options.c: Resistance is caused by drinking antibiotics
options.d: Bacteria become resistant by becoming larger

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.questionText: Scenario #3 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, in a Mendelian dihybrid cross of AaBb × AaBb, what is the expected phenotypic ratio among the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: Dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb (independent assortment) gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio — 9 dominant both : 3 dominant A, recessive b : 3 recessive a, dominant B : 1 recessive both.

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, where is the hormone adrenaline produced in the human body?

options.a: Thyroid gland (in the neck)
options.b: Adrenal glands (situated above the kidneys)
options.c: Pituitary gland (at the base of the brain)
options.d: Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)

questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is produced by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of each kidney. It increases heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose in 'fight or flight' situations.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly distinguishes phenotype from genotype?

options.a: Phenotype and genotype are identical
options.b: Phenotype is the allele composition
options.c: Genotype is the visible appearance
options.d: Phenotype is the observable trait (e.g., tall plant); genotype is the genetic makeup (e.g., Tt)

questions.explanation: Phenotype: the observable characteristic (tall, short, red, etc.). Genotype: the genetic makeup (allele combination: e.g., TT, Tt, tt). Different genotypes can produce the same phenotype (e.g., TT and Tt both result in tall plants).
